sections.overview: The European storm petrel is one of the smallest seabirds of the North Atlantic. It spends nearly its whole life over the open ocean and comes ashore only in summer, at night, to nest on remote islands.
sections.identification: A bird barely larger than a house martin, about 14–18 cm long with a wingspan of 36–39 cm; adults weigh around 26 g. The plumage is dark brownish-black with a broad white patch on the rump and a pale band under each wing. The tail is short and square-ended, unlike the forked tail of Leach’s petrel, and the small bill has a tube on top.
sections.habitat: It lives almost entirely at sea. In summer it breeds on remote, small, rat-free offshore islands and a few isolated headlands on the Atlantic fringe of north and west Britain and Ireland. Outside the breeding season it is best seen from headlands in autumn, when onshore winds bring birds closer to land.
sections.diet: It picks small fish, crustaceans and plankton from the sea surface. It feeds by fluttering low over the waves with its wings held in a V, its webbed feet pattering on the water so that it seems to run across it. A good sense of smell helps it find food over open ocean.
sections.behavior: It visits its colonies only at night and nests underground, and it often stays at sea on bright moonlit nights, which makes it hard to see in the breeding season. From its burrow it sings a purring call mixed with grunts and squeaks. At sea it often feeds in flocks and follows ships, especially trawlers.
sections.reproduction: A pair lays a single egg, incubated by both sexes for 38–50 days. The downy chick stays in the nest for 56–73 days before fledging. There is typically one brood a year, and breeding typically starts at about four years of age. The nest is made among rocks or in a burrow.
sections.ecology: The storm petrel feeds on small animals of the surface waters and depends on healthy seas. Colonies are found mainly on islands free of rats and other mammalian predators, which threaten eggs and chicks.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern, and it is Amber-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was about 26,000 nests in 1998–2002, with an uncertain trend, though some colonies have grown, with a doubling on Mousa. It is long-lived: the oldest ringed bird reached over 38 years.
